page: Amazon Web Services r5.4xlarge is a memory-optimized virtual machine built on the AWS Nitro hypervisor architecture. The instance is powered by an Intel Xeon Platinum 8259CL processor operating at a base frequency of 3.1 GHz. Compute resources include 16 dedicated virtual CPUs split across 8 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading. Hardware instruction support spans AVX, AVX-512F, AES cryptography extensions, and bit-manipulation sets, backed by 35 MB of shared L3 cache.

Memory capacity is a core differentiator, providing 128 GB of DDR4 RAM clocked at 3 GHz. This configuration maintains a high 8:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio, yielding 8 GB of RAM per vCPU. Storage architecture contains no bundled local disks, relying entirely on remote Elastic Block Store volumes for operating system and data requirements. Baseline networking throughput is provisioned at 5 Gbps, with zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses included. No dedicated GPU hardware is present on this instance type.

Benchmark testing reveals an architecture suited for concurrent execution rather than single-threaded speed. In stress-ng and Geekbench evaluations, single-core CPU throughput ranks in the lower quartile, whereas multi-core execution settles firmly in the middle tier with 13,542 points in stress-ng and 6,589 points in Geekbench. PassMark testing mirrors these results, generating an overall CPU score of 14,402.83 and database processing scores of 5,440.76. Uncached memory read bandwidth reaches 79.24 GB/sec, while write operations sustain 48.62 GB/sec. Redis caching benchmarks achieve 13.23 million SET operations per second, indicating consistent memory subsystem responsiveness.

From an infrastructure efficiency standpoint, the r5.4xlarge prioritizes memory allocation density over raw per-core frequency. Applications with intense single-thread constraints may experience throughput limitations, but multi-threaded workloads benefit from balanced parallel execution. The instance serves production environments running in-memory databases such as Redis and Memcached, relational databases requiring substantial buffer caches, distributed caching layers, real-time data mining, and enterprise memory-bound data pipelines.
